report.source_text: Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone revealed a large mass of mixed density with cystic and solid components. It was ill-defined and infiltrative and had an extensively enhancing component extending to the left petrous apex and left side of the clivus. There was an inferior extension to the left infratemporal fossa and nasopharyngeal and parapharyngeal spaces, displacing the nasopharynx anteriorly with adjacent airway narrowing without mucosal invasion. The lesion extended to the left mastoid air cells and middle ear cavity. It infiltrated the left jugular bulb and inferiorly extended to the proximal jugular vein with non-opacification, invasion, and significant osseous destruction of the left petrous bone and occipital condyle. Dehiscence, left carotid canal resorption, and left jugular foramen widening were also observed (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).

clinician.final_diagnosis: Left petrous internal carotid artery (ICA) dissection aneurysm
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 60-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis and prior stroke (with left facial palsy and hemiparesis) presented with 4 months of left ear discharge, decreased hearing, and non-pulsatile tinnitus. She was initially referred to otolaryngology for management of what was suspected to be an aggressive left glomus jugulare based on initial imaging. CT of the temporal bone revealed a large infiltrative mass with mixed density, cystic and solid components, extensively enhancing, extending to the left petrous apex and clivus, with osseous destruction of the petrous bone and occipital condyle, carotid canal resorption, and jugular foramen widening with jugular vein involvement. MRI confirmed a large heterogeneous mixed cystic and soft tissue lesion extending to the left petrous apex, with the cystic component showing high T2/FLAIR signal and the soft tissue component showing isointense signal without diffusion restriction. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated hypointensity of the lesion with hyperattenuation on apparent diffusion coefficient sequences, findings more consistent with an aneurysm than a solid tumor. CT angiography subsequently identified the true diagnosis: a left petrous ICA dissection aneurysm. The patient underwent endovascular treatment with stenting of the petrous ICA and carotid angioplasty using a hyperglide balloon, achieving successful deployment with clear flow diversion away from the aneurysm and desirable stagnation within the aneurysm sac.

She was initially referred to otolaryngology for management of what was suspected to be an aggressive left glomus jugulare based on initial imaging. CT of the temporal bone revealed a large infiltrative mass with mixed density, cystic and solid components, extensively enhancing, extending to the left petrous apex and clivus, with osseous destruction of the petrous bone and occipital condyle, carotid canal resorption, and jugular foramen widening with jugular vein involvement. MRI confirmed a large heterogeneous mixed cystic and soft tissue lesion extending to the left petrous apex, with the cystic component showing high T2/FLAIR signal and the soft tissue component showing isointense signal without diffusion restriction. MRI diffusion-weighted imaging demonstrated hypointensity of the lesion with hyperattenuation on apparent diffusion coefficient sequences, findings more consistent with an aneurysm than a solid tumor. CT angiography subsequently identified the true diagnosis: a left petrous ICA dissection aneurysm. The patient underwent endovascular treatment with stenting of the petrous ICA and carotid angioplasty using a hyperglide balloon, achieving successful deployment with clear flow diversion away from the aneurysm and desirable stagnation within the aneurysm sac.

Patient has chronic kidney disease on hemodialysis and prior stroke with left facial palsy and hemiparesis

CT temporal bone showed large infiltrative mass with mixed density, cystic and solid components, extensively enhancing, extending to left petrous apex and clivus, with osseous destruction of petrous bone and occipital condyle, carotid canal resorption, jugular foramen widening, and jugular vein involvement

MRI revealed large heterogeneous mixed cystic and soft tissue lesion extending to left petrous apex with high T2/FLAIR signal in cystic component and isointense soft tissue without diffusion restriction
MRI diffusion-weighted imaging showed hypointensity of the aneurysm with hyperattenuation on apparent diffusion coefficient sequence
CT angiography identified left petrous ICA dissection aneurysm (known final diagnosis)
Endovascular treatment with stenting of petrous ICA and carotid angioplasty was performed with successful deployment, clear flow diversion away from aneurysm, and desirable stagnation within aneurysm

ruled_out_or_less_likely_alternatives.basis: Initial clinical presentation and temporal bone CT findings (osseous destruction, jugular vein involvement, carotid canal resorption) were initially interpreted as glomus jugulare. However, MRI diffusion-weighted imaging showing hypointensity with ADC hyperattenuation is more consistent with an aneurysm than a solid vascular tumor. CT angiography confirmed the diagnosis of ICA dissection aneurysm rather than glomus jugulare.
